title: Does an Executable Validator Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that measured whether inserting an executable emulator validator (with a bounded one-iteration repair policy) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow. We used a deterministic shared-generation paired design on N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class) with a single shared generator candidate per task produced by gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120). A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applied structured workflow policies (for example, make-before-break, must_be_down_for_fields) and could request ≤1 repair. Observed outcomes: baseline successes = 120/120; guarded successes = 120/120 (paired contingency n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0). Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We revise the manuscript to (1) present a compact formal definition of the binary scoring rule used in the confirmatory test with a representative pass example from archived artifacts and note the absence of archived fails in this run; (2) add a concise nearest-work comparison that clarifies how our shared-generation paired design isolates validator effects relative to prior generator-focused studies; and (3) tighten experimental framing and methodological recommendations for follow-ups when generator-induced errors are rare.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate operator intent into low-level network configuration commands, promising productivity gains for NetOps. However, syntactically plausible commands can violate workflow invariants (for example sequencing or availability constraints) and cause semantic failures that only appear under closed-loop execution. Prior work therefore proposes verification, emulation (digital twins), or veto layers to detect hazardous changes before enactment. We study the marginal effect of an executable validator plus a bounded repair policy on identical generator outputs. Our preregistered research question is: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To answer this precisely we used a shared-generation paired design: for each task a single generator output was evaluated both as baseline (LLM-only suggestion) and as guarded (validator ± repair). This isolates validator/repair effects by holding generator variance constant, at the cost that if the generator rarely produces invalid candidates the guarded path will be idle. We report the preregistered confirmatory test results, add a compact formalization of the pass–fail mapping used in the McNemar test, and provide concrete methodological recommendations for future runs targeting repair utility.
sections.related_work: Two strands are most relevant. First, executable closed-loop benchmarks and emulation-based verification (representative examples: NetConfArena and other closed-loop emulation benchmarks) show that text- or syntax-level correctness misses stateful errors (make-before-break mistakes, group-availability violations, ordering constraints). Second, tool-augmented and bounded-autonomy architectures (generate→validate→repair, veto layers, translation-to-formal-model, canary enactments) have been proposed and prototyped to improve safety. Prior experiments commonly mix generator variance and validator effects (independent generation per condition), which answers a different question—How often does a generator produce safe outputs under a prompting strategy?—than our validator-focused question—Given the same generator output, can a validator/repair subsystem prevent semantic failures? We therefore place our work as a complementary experimental lens: it isolates the marginal effect of validation/repair on identical generator outputs and is most informative when generators produce a nontrivial fraction of invalid candidates.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1 before execution. Primary design: paired binary confirmatory test with N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks (40 per topology class: edge/core/leaf–spine). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Prespecified test: exact two-sided McNemar; paired-difference CI by bootstrap-percentile (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistration defined deterministic task generation, deterministic emulator resets, contamination rules, and a bounded repair budget (≤1 repair per guarded episode). Execution summary (from archived manifests): planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared initial generation per pair); declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini; validator_id = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0); preregistration_sha256 = 0bfc96e9afceed579f04a06dcbad2387ee4acca970559d9a4faa165893f4fe50.

Task generation and validator semantics. Tasks were produced deterministically (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) and include initial_state, expected_final_state, a natural-language intent, and an explicit required_sequence (canonical ordered operations). The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5: this executable emulator enforces task-encoded workflow policies (examples: must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break) by simulating candidate enactment and emitting a structured validator_trace with fields including validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied. Repair policy: when validator.violation_count>0 the preregistered repair procedure could request one repair iteration from the generator; repair prompts and provider traces were archived when generated.

Formal binary outcome definition (compact). The confirmatory test used a binary pass/fail label per episode defined as:
- PASS (label = 1): validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true AND validator_trace.violation_count == 0; scorer reported score == 1 under scoring_rule == "full_intent_constraint_validation".
- FAIL (label = 0): validator_trace.violation_count > 0 OR scorer reported score != 1.
This mapping is deterministic given the archived validator_trace and scorer fields; it was applied identically to baseline and guarded episodes. Representative archived pass example (task-000001, baseline): normalized_response == "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up"; score = 1; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; validator_trace.violation_count = 0; hence PASS. No archived FAIL examples exist because every episode produced validator.violation_count = 0; consequently no repair_provider_trace artifacts were generated in this run. The absence of archived fails is an empirical outcome we analyze below.

Contamination controls and reconciliation. The harness enforced deterministic emulator resets (container-image checksums + deterministic seeds), duplicate-output detection, and provider-call audits. Contamination summary and missingness artifacts report zero exclusions; the deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirms pair accounting (n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0) and hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 (cache_miss_count = 120). All execution and analysis artifacts used in these statements are archived and checksummed in the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Primary confirmatory outcome. The run completed with complete_pair_count = 120. Condition-level totals (analysis/condition_summary.csv) record baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is:
- n_11 (both success) = 120
- n_10 (guarded success, baseline fail) = 0
- n_01 (baseline success, guarded fail) = 0
- n_00 (both fail) = 0
Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces report repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; therefore secondary endpoints measuring repair incidence are vacuous in this run.

Per-topology counts (preregistered partition). Each topology class had 40 tasks and identical outcomes per class:
- Edge (40 tasks): baseline 40/40 success; guarded 40/40 success.
- Core (40 tasks): baseline 40/40 success; guarded 40/40 success.
- Leaf–spine (40 tasks): baseline 40/40 success; guarded 40/40 success.
These per-topology counts are present in representative scoring artifacts (for example execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json) and analysis/condition_summary.csv.

Diagnostics and artifact observations. Representative scoring artifacts show normalized_response equals normalized_reference_answer, parsed_command_count equals required_command_count from the task payload, validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, validator_trace.repair_applied = false, validator_id = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, validator_version = 5.0. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120; deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms provider-call audits and pair accounting are internally consistent. The observed degenerate CI is a direct statistical consequence of zero discordant pairs under the preregistered resampling procedure (bootstrap resamples reproduce the identical paired table).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and design trade-offs. The shared-generation paired design cleanly isolates the marginal effect of a validator/repair subsystem on identical generator outputs. However, that very isolation means the guarded subsystem has no opportunity to act if the generator output is already valid under the validator's policy encoding; this is precisely what occurred: the generator produced valid candidates for all 120 tasks, so validator.violation_count was never >0 and repairs were never invoked. Statistically, zero discordant pairs render the McNemar test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size (the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline failure rate ≈0.40). The observed outcome therefore documents a ceiling effect for this task bank and generator configuration, not a general statement that validators are unnecessary in broader settings.

Nearest-work comparison (compact). We summarize closest prior empirical/benchmark efforts and highlight contrasts with our study:
- Protogeros et al., "Benchmarking LLM-Driven Network Configuration Repair" (arXiv:2604.22513): generator-centered benchmark that measures repair success across model draws; typically uses independent generation per condition. Contrast: our paired shared-generation design holds generator output fixed to isolate validator effects.
- NetConfArena (arXiv:2608.23179): executable closed-loop benchmark that emphasizes end-to-end emulation-based failure detection. Contrast: NetConfArena focuses on generator variance across tasks; our contribution is a preregistered paired protocol to isolate validator marginal effects and the associated artifact accounting.
- MeshAgent (DOI:10.1145/3771567) and Lightyear (DOI:10.1145/3603269.3604842): tools and verification frameworks that demonstrate reachability and configuration verification at scale. Contrast: these works emphasize tool capability and scaling; our experiment assesses the guarded pipeline's incremental effect on identical generator outputs under a bounded repair policy.
This compact matrix clarifies that our methodological contribution is orthogonal to generator benchmarking: we show how a shared-generation paired design and deterministic archived validator traces enable unambiguous attribution of outcomes to the validator/repair subsystem when generator variance is controlled.

Practical recommendations for follow-ups. To measure repair utility when generators seldom err, we recommend preregistered design adjustments: (1) independent generation per condition or a hybrid blocked design to allow guarded pipelines to intercept generator-induced errors; (2) targeted selection of high-difficulty tasks (for example tasks labeled "very_hard" or with high dependency_rule_count in the task manifest) to increase the prior probability of generator violations; (3) controlled prompt perturbations (the preregistration included exploratory perturbation variants) applied deterministically to prespecified task subsets; (4) an exploratory arm with expanded repair budgets (multiple repair iterations) to study repair convergence and cost. The archived task_manifest difficulty fields support deterministic selection rules for such follow-ups without changing harness semantics.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strong (deterministic resets, complete provider-call audits, zero exclusions). Construct validity is limited by validator policy encodings derived from synthetic task payloads (some vendor or partial-observability behaviors are not modeled). External validity is constrained by the synthetic curated task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power scenario assumed substantial baseline failure; observed baseline = 0 contradicts that assumption and makes the primary test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable validator-plus-bounded-repair pipeline to an LLM-only suggestion workflow under a deterministic shared-generation design using gpt-5-mini. All shared initial candidates passed the emulator validator, producing concordant successes in baseline and guarded conditions (n_11 = 120) and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The principal scientific contribution is methodological: we demonstrate how a preregistered shared-generation paired protocol with deterministic validator traces and reconciliation artifacts cleanly attributes outcomes to validator/repair subsystems and yields artifact-grounded recommendations for future confirmatory designs when generator-induced failures are rare. Follow-up studies that relax shared-generation, stratify on task difficulty, introduce controlled prompt perturbations, or expand repair budgets are needed to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
